passage: As her mother, I nagged Trisha about her phone for months. "Enough now," I'd call from the kitchen, and she'd say "five minutes", and those five minutes lasted till dinner. Then one afternoon I just watched instead of talking. She came home, dropped her bag, sat on the sofa, and the phone was in her hand before her shoes were off. The sofa was the start of it, every time. So I didn't lecture. I asked her to help me move the charging point from the sofa table to the shelf in my room, and we put a bowl of fruit and her sketchbook on the sofa instead. The first week she grumbled. By the third, she was sketching while she ate. I'm Deepika, by the way. I still nag, but much less.

qa.q: Where did Deepika and Trisha move the charging point?
qa.a: From the sofa table to the shelf in Deepika's room.

qa.q: Why might Trisha have said "five minutes" and then kept scrolling till dinner?
qa.a: She probably meant it and felt confident she could stop, but the sofa set off the habit so strongly that the phone kept her before she noticed time passing.

qa.q: What choice did Deepika make instead of nagging, and why did it work?
qa.a: She changed the setting, moving the charger away and putting fruit and the sketchbook on the sofa, so the old cue led to something new.

qa.q: What was the change like for Trisha?
qa.a: At first Trisha grumbled at losing the easy phone spot, but by the third week she was sketching while she ate, without being told off.

grounding: A mother notices that her daughter's phone habit starts on the sofa and changes the setting rather than nagging.

Note for Nandini's school counsellor, from her mother, Farida
You asked me to notice when the phone habit starts, so I watched for a week without saying anything. It is almost always the same: Nandini comes in from school, sits in the big armchair by the window, and within a minute the phone is out. On the days she sits at the dining table instead, she eats and talks to me first. On Wednesday I moved the armchair to the balcony door and put the charger in the hallway. I didn't make a speech about it. She noticed, frowned, and sat at the table. We talked about her science teacher for twenty minutes. I will keep this setup for another week and tell you how it goes. I think the chair was doing more than I realised.

qa.a: To the balcony door, and the charger went into the hallway.

qa.q: What does Nandini's frown suggest she felt about the change?
qa.a: She was probably a little annoyed or thrown off to find her usual spot gone, yet the frown passed and she chose to sit at the table.

qa.q: Which choice by Farida worked better than nagging, and why?
qa.a: Watching quietly for a week, then moving the armchair and charger without a speech; changing the place removed the cue without starting a fight.

qa.q: How might the school counsellor read Farida's note?
qa.a: The counsellor would see a parent who looked for the pattern first and tested a small change, which gives useful evidence for helping Nandini further.

grounding: A mother watches her daughter's after-school phone habit, spots the armchair as its cue, and changes the setting instead of nagging.

14 Nov, night
Something clicked today. For weeks I've been snapping at Nirmala, "Phone down!", and she rolls her eyes and nothing changes. Today I came home early and saw exactly how it starts. She walked in, flopped on the diwan by the TV, and reached for the phone lying on the cushion, like her hand knew the way. She wasn't choosing anything. The diwan was choosing. So this evening I asked if she'd help me turn the diwan into a reading corner: a lamp, her comics, and the phone basket moved to the dining shelf. She thought I'd lost my mind. But she helped, and tonight she read two chapters there before she even remembered the phone. We'll see tomorrow. No more snapping from me.
Gurpreet (Papa)

passage: Every day after school, Nitin waited in the staff room at St Joseph's for his mother Bidisha to finish her last class. Dear Sabina,

You asked how things are with Hiba and the phone. Better, and not because I shouted.

I watched her for a week, pretending to read the paper. She walks in, throws her bag down, drops onto the sofa, and in two seconds she's scrolling. It isn't a choice. The sofa is the switch.

So on Sunday I moved the phone basket to the dining table, next to a plate of fruit. When she gets home, phones go in the basket, she eats at the table, and homework starts there. The sofa is for after.

She sulked for two days. Then on Thursday she said, "It's weird, I don't even miss it till later." I nearly dropped my tea 😄

Your advice about not nagging helped. Come see us soon.

Zainab

You asked what finally worked with my son and his phone, Jasleen. It wasn't lecturing. I'm Anjali, and I'd been nagging for a year.
Then I just watched him for a week, without saying anything. Every day it was the same: he'd walk in from school, drop his bag, sink onto the sofa, and in the same second the phone was in his hand. Two hours gone. The sofa was the trigger.
So I stopped nagging and changed the room. We moved the charger to the kitchen. I put a bowl of fruit and his sketchbook on the dining table, where the light is good. He sits there now for the first half hour, eating and drawing.
He still uses his phone. But it isn't the first thing anymore. I felt so silly for nagging all that time, when the sofa was doing half the work.

qa.a: Anjali moved the charger to the kitchen.

qa.a: Anjali felt a bit silly and regretful for nagging so long, and relieved to find a simpler way.

qa.q: Why did changing the room work better than nagging?
qa.a: It removed the cue that started the phone habit and made another activity easier, so Anjali's son didn't need willpower.

qa.q: How might Anjali's son feel about the new after-school setup?
qa.a: He probably feels less nagged and more at ease, since he can snack and draw without an argument.

I'm Rashmi, Ramesh's mother, and I'll just describe what I saw, because I'm still not sure what goes on in his head.
Every day at 3:40, the school bus drops Ramesh at the gate. By 3:45 he's on the sofa with the phone. Not deciding. Just there, like a key turning a lock. By six, homework is untouched and he looks dull and cranky.
I used to shout. It made things worse. He'd say, “Just five more minutes,” and five became fifty.
So one weekend, I moved the sofa to the other wall and put the study table by the window where it had been. I left the charger in my room.
On Monday he came in, stopped, looked confused, then sat at the table because that's what was in front of him. He opened his maths book before he even reached for his pocket.
I don't know if it'll last. But it's the first calm evening in months.

Vinita's flat in Dharavi had one room, one sofa and one plug point beside it. Every afternoon, her daughter Keerthana came in from school, sat on the sofa, plugged in her phone and did not look up until dinner.
Vinita, who stitched blouses at the machine by the door, had shouted about it for a month. It never worked. Keerthana would just say, "Two minutes, Amma," and two minutes lasted till eight.
One afternoon, sewing a hem, Vinita watched closely. Keerthana's hand reached for the phone the exact moment her back touched the sofa. Not before. Not after.
There was no space for a study table. So that night, Vinita pushed the sofa to the other wall, away from the only plug point, and put a stool and a lamp where it had been. She ran a long wire to the kitchen for the phone charger.
The next day, Keerthana stood in the middle of the room, confused. Then she sat on the stool and opened her book.

qa.q: Where did Vinita put the phone charger?
qa.a: She ran a long wire to the kitchen for it.

qa.q: What was Vinita thinking as she watched Keerthana sit down?
qa.a: She realised with some relief that the habit started the exact moment Keerthana's back touched the sofa, which meant the setting, not only Keerthana, was driving it.

qa.q: Why did moving the sofa work better than shouting?
qa.a: It removed the cue that started the loop, sofa plus plug point, so Keerthana did not have to fight the habit with willpower.

qa.q: How does Keerthana feel walking into the changed room?
qa.a: Keerthana feels confused at first, standing in the middle of the room, before settling onto the stool with her book.

On Monday, Rashmi walked in, looked for the beanbag and frowned. "Papa, where's..."
"Balcony. For weekends."
She stood there, then dropped into the chair by the window. The chikki bowl was right there. Her maths book came out before the phone did.
